runs.text:
Inline object prop creates a new object identity on every parent render:

```jsx
<Child options={{ sort: "name" }} />
```

Even if contents match, `{} !== {}`. React sees prop changed -> `Child` re-renders, especially with `React.memo`.

Fix: memoize object or pass primitives.

```jsx
const options = useMemo(() => ({ sort: "name" }), []);

return <Child options={options} />;
```

If object depends on state:

```jsx
const options = useMemo(() => ({ sort }), [sort]);
```

Rule: stable refs for object/array/function props when child render cost matters.

Because inline object literal creates a new ref on every parent render:

```jsx
<Child options={{ theme, size }} />
```

React compares props by identity. New object ref -> prop changed -> memoized child still re-renders.

Fix: memoize object in parent:

```jsx
const options = useMemo(() => ({ theme, size }), [theme, size]);

return <Child options={options} />;
```

Also wrap child only if needed:

```jsx
export default React.memo(Child);
```

Rule: inline objects/arrays/functions are “new” every render. Use `useMemo` / `useCallback`, or pass primitives directly.

`git merge`: combines branches by adding a merge commit. Preserves true history.

Use when:
- Shared branch / team branch
- You want audit trail of how work joined
- Avoid rewriting history

Risk:
- History gets noisier
- Conflict resolution happens once, but merge commits can pile up

`git rebase`: moves your commits onto a new base, rewriting commit history. Creates linear history.

Use when:
- Your local feature branch needs latest `main`
- Before opening PR, to clean history
- Branch is not shared, or team agrees rewriting is OK

Risk:
- Rewrites commit hashes
- Dangerous on shared branches: others may get broken history
- Conflicts may happen commit-by-commit
- Bad rebase can drop/duplicate commits if handled carelessly

Rule of thumb:

- Private branch: `rebase`
- Shared branch: `merge`
- Unsure: `merge` is safer.

`git merge`: preserves branch history. Adds a merge commit tying branches together. Use for shared branches, PR integration, release branches, or when you want exact historical context. Risk: noisier graph, harder linear reading.

`git rebase`: rewrites your branch commits onto a new base. Creates linear history. Use on your own local feature branch before PR, or to refresh against `main`. Risk: rewritten commit hashes; dangerous after pushing/shared work because collaborators can get duplicate/diverged commits.

Rule: rebase private work, merge shared work.

Conflict risk exists in both. Rebase may make you resolve conflicts commit-by-commit; merge usually resolves once. Never rebase public/shared branches unless team explicitly agrees.

Before splitting, evaluate:

- Actual bottleneck: DB queries, cache, Celery, N+1s, slow views, infra, deployment, not “monolith” by default.
- Domain boundaries: clear bounded contexts, ownership, data lifecycle.
- Data coupling: shared tables, transactions, joins, consistency needs.
- Team structure: independent teams? On-call? service ownership?
- Operational maturity: observability, CI/CD, tracing, retries, idempotency, SLOs.
- Release pain: are teams blocked by shared deploys, or just slow tests/builds?
- Failure model: network calls, partial failure, timeouts, version skew.
- Auth/security: cross-service authz, secrets, audit, tenant isolation.
- Cost: infra, latency, debugging, duplicated code, migrations.
- Alternatives first: modular monolith, app boundaries, DB indexing, async jobs, caching, read replicas, test parallelism.

Rule: split only when a module has clear ownership, clear API, low data coupling, independent scaling/deploy need, and the team can operate it. Otherwise, modularize the Django monolith first.

Use one atomic SQL statement:

```sql
UPDATE counters
SET value = value + 1
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING value;
```

Node `pg`:

```js
const { rows } = await pool.query(
  `UPDATE counters
   SET value = value + 1
   WHERE id = $1
   RETURNING value`,
  [counterId]
);

res.json({ value: rows[0].value });
```

Avoid this race:

```js
SELECT value FROM counters;
UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1;
```

That splits read/write, so concurrent reqs can read same old value.

Postgres row-level lock from `UPDATE` serializes increments. `RETURNING` gives the committed incremented value for that request.

If counter row may not exist, use atomic upsert:

```sql
INSERT INTO counters (id, value)
VALUES ($1, 1)
ON CONFLICT (id)
DO UPDATE SET value = counters.value + 1
RETURNING value;
```

Use one atomic SQL statement:

```sql
UPDATE counters
SET value = value + 1
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING value;
```

Node:

```js
const { rows } = await pool.query(
  `UPDATE counters
   SET value = value + 1
   WHERE id = $1
   RETURNING value`,
  [counterId]
);

res.json({ value: rows[0].value });
```

Do not do:

```js
SELECT value ...
UPDATE counters SET value = selected + 1 ...
```

That read-modify-write path races. `UPDATE ... SET value = value + 1 RETURNING value` is atomic in PostgreSQL; concurrent reqs serialize on the row lock, each gets a unique incremented value.
